title: Speculating about the past
tagline: How sure are you? English has a modal for every shade of certainty about something already over.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (MUST, CAN'T, MIGHT, BEEN, SHOULD, THOUGHT)
Reading & Use of English Part 1 — multiple-choice cloze (must/can't/might + have + participle)
Writing Part 1 — formal report or proposal: hedged speculation about causes and outcomes
Speaking Part 3 — negotiating explanations for something that happened off-screen
why: Speculating about the past is a daily conversational skill dressed up as grammar: deciding, from the evidence, how sure you actually are. C1 candidates need the full range — from a flat impossibility (can't have) to a hedged academic guess (it is thought that) — and Use of English checks the exact auxiliary and participle each modal demands, including the continuous forms that show an activity, not just a finished fact.

diagrams.title: Speculating about an ongoing past activity

parts.chip: a guess about a completed or ongoing past event

diagrams.caption: Add been + -ing to shift the guess from a finished fact to an activity still in progress at that past moment.

diagrams.title: Hedging a guess for formal writing

before.text: The ancient civilisation must have abandoned the site because of drought.

after.text: It seems likely that the ancient civilisation abandoned the site because of drought.

steps: Replace the modal + have + participle with a hedging phrase: it seems likely that / it is thought that / presumably.
Move the speculated verb into an ordinary past tense inside the that-clause.
This register shift is typical of academic or formal reports, where a bare modal can sound too casual, or too certain.

formula.chip: must / can't / couldn't / may / might / could + have (been) + participle
a speculation about a completed or ongoing past event

head: Pattern
Meaning
Example
rows: the noise could have been the wind
a guess about an ongoing past activity
she must have been waiting for hours
an expected outcome, not yet confirmed
the parcel should have arrived by now
an arrangement whose outcome is uncertain or didn't happen
the report was to have been finished by Monday
it is thought that the fire started accidentally

examples.text: The lights are off and the car's gone — they must have left already.
examples.note: must have = a confident deduction from clear evidence

examples.text: He can't have read the whole novel in one night — it's nearly 900 pages.
examples.note: can't have = a confident negative deduction

examples.text: She couldn't have known about the surprise; we only decided this morning.
examples.note: couldn't have = impossible, given the facts

use.point: May/might/could have for genuine, open uncertainty

examples.text: They may have taken a different route — that would explain the delay.
examples.note: may have = a real, open possibility

examples.text: The message might have gone to your spam folder.
examples.note: might have = uncertain, slightly more tentative than may

examples.text: The strange sound could have been the pipes, or just the wind.
examples.note: could have = one possibility among several

examples.text: Judging by the mud on her boots, she must have been walking for hours.
examples.note: continuous form for an ongoing past activity

examples.text: He looked shattered — he might have been training since dawn.
examples.note: might have been + -ing = a tentative guess about an ongoing activity

use.point: Should/ought to have and was/were to have for expected or uncertain outcomes; hedged speculation

examples.text: The bus should have arrived by now — I hope nothing's wrong.
examples.note: should have = expected, but not yet confirmed

examples.text: The bridge was to have been completed last year, but funding ran out.
examples.note: was to have + participle = an arrangement whose outcome was uncertain, or never happened

examples.text: It is thought that the settlement was abandoned due to a prolonged drought.
examples.note: hedged speculation, typical of formal or academic writing

watch_out.why: The auxiliary after a modal is always have, never had, regardless of tense.

watch_out.wrong: He can't have forget the meeting.
watch_out.why: Use the past participle after can't have, not the base form.

watch_out.wrong: They might have arrive late because of the traffic.
watch_out.right: They might have arrived late because of the traffic.
watch_out.why: Might have needs the past participle, not the bare infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: She must have wait for hours in that queue.
watch_out.right: She must have been waiting for hours in that queue.
watch_out.why: An ongoing past activity needs the continuous form: modal + have been + -ing.

watch_out.wrong: The results should have publish yesterday.
watch_out.right: The results should have been published yesterday.
watch_out.why: A passive event needs should have been + participle, not the base form.

watch_out.wrong: I am sure the fire started deliberately.
watch_out.right: It is thought that the fire started deliberately.
watch_out.why: Formal or academic writing prefers a hedged structure to a flat, unsupported claim.

dialogue.title: The mystery of the locked classroom
dialogue.context: Ten minutes before the lesson, Miss Vega's classroom is locked and dark, and the students speculate about what has happened.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: The door's locked and the lights are off. Where's Miss Vega?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: She must have forgotten it's Tuesday — we have double English today.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: No, she's never late. Something must have happened.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: She can't have gone home; her car's still in the car park.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Maybe she's in a meeting. The head might have called an emergency staff meeting.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Or she could have been held up marking our essays — there were a lot this week.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Look at Nadia's face — she must have been waiting outside the staffroom, listening.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Fine, I overheard something. The heating should have been fixed this morning, apparently it wasn't.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: So the whole meeting was to have lasted ten minutes and ran over?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Exactly. Officially, it is thought that the boiler failed overnight.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Well, that explains why she couldn't have texted us — no signal in that old building.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Mystery solved. Let's just wait quietly.

items.sentence: The lights are off and her coat's gone — she ___ home already.
items.why: must have = a confident deduction from clear evidence

items.sentence: He ___ finished the marathon in two hours — he can barely run to the bus stop.
items.why: can't have = a confident negative deduction, near-impossible

items.sentence: I'm not sure why the light's flashing — it ___ a low battery.
items.why: might have been = a genuinely uncertain possibility

items.sentence: Her hair's soaking wet — she ___ in the rain without an umbrella.
items.why: modal + have been + -ing for a guess about an ongoing past activity

items.sentence: The parcel ___ by Friday, according to the tracking information, but it still hasn't.
items.why: should have = an expected outcome, not yet confirmed

items.sentence: The ceremony ___ finished by six, but nobody has confirmed whether it actually did.
items.why: was to have = an arrangement whose outcome is uncertain

items.sentence: Historians believe the fortress ___ abandoned after the earthquake, though no records survive.
items.why: hedged speculation, typical of formal or academic writing

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct form of the word(s) in brackets.

items.sentence: She ___ (must / leave) already — her coat's gone.
He ___ (can't / finish) the marathon that fast — he can barely run to the bus stop.
The light was flashing oddly — it ___ (might / have) a low battery.
Her hair's soaking wet — she ___ (must / walk) in the rain for a while.
The parcel ___ (should / arrive) by Friday, according to the tracking information.
The ceremony ___ (be to / finish) by six, but nobody has confirmed it.
Historians believe the fortress ___ (thought / abandon) after the earthquake.
answers: is thought to have been abandoned

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: I'm sure she left already, because her coat isn't here.
It's impossible that he finished the marathon that fast.
Perhaps the delay was caused by roadworks — nobody's sure.
Judging by the noise outside, someone was probably mowing the lawn for a long time.
items.second_end: the lawn for a long time.

items.first: I expected the results to be published yesterday, but I haven't checked.
Experts believe the bridge collapsed because of metal fatigue, although this is not confirmed.

summary: Must/can't/couldn't have + participle express confident deductions — positive certainty and its negative mirror.
May/might/could have + participle express genuine, open uncertainty about the past.
Modal + have been + -ing speculates about an activity in progress at some past moment, not just a completed fact.
Should/ought to have and was/were to have both describe an expected outcome whose result is unconfirmed, or never happened.
Formal and academic writing hedges speculation with phrases like it is thought that, rather than a bare modal.
